whyCorrect: Let s be the price of one stave and h the price of one hoop, so 8s + 3h = 131 and 5s + 6h = 152. Double the first equation to get 16s + 6h = 262, then subtract the second so the hoops cancel: 11s = 110, giving s = 10. Substituting back gives 3h = 131 - 80 = 51, so h = 17. Six staves and two hoops therefore cost 6(10) + 2(17) = 60 + 34 = 94.

whyWrong.B: 104 is 7(10) + 2(17): the prices are right but seven staves are counted instead of the six the question asks for.
whyWrong.C: 112 satisfies neither order: with the stave price of 10 it needs a hoop price of 26, but then 5(10) + 6(26) = 206, not 152. It is the value you land on by fitting prices to only one of the two orders.
whyWrong.D: 122 is 6(17) + 2(10): the two prices have been swapped, so the hoop price is charged for the staves.

commonMistakes: Solving for s and h and then stopping, instead of pricing the new order the question actually asks about.
tips: Match the coefficients of one variable before subtracting; here doubling the first equation lines up the 6h in both.

whyCorrect: The shadow shortens at a constant rate, so find that rate first: it lost 96 - 51 = 45 centimetres over the 3 hours from 8:00 to 11:00, which is 15 centimetres per hour. Starting from 96 centimetres, the length after t hours is 96 - 15t. Set 96 - 15t = 21, so 15t = 75 and t = 5.

whyWrong.A: 4 hours gives 96 - 60 = 36 centimetres, not 21; it is the answer if you measure from 51 centimetres at 11:00 but then report the time since 8:00.
whyWrong.C: 6 hours gives 96 - 90 = 6 centimetres, overshooting the target length.
whyWrong.D: 8 is the clock hour the shadow reaches 21 centimetres (1:00 in the afternoon is 5 hours after 8:00), not the number of hours asked for; it also matches dividing 96 by a rate of 12.

commonMistakes: Using 45 centimetres per hour instead of dividing that loss by the 3 hours it took.

whyCorrect: The fixed mass aboard is 195 for the pilot and basket plus 2(74) = 148 for the passengers, which is 343 kilograms. That leaves 480 - 343 = 137 kilograms for ballast. Each bag is 18 kilograms, and \(\frac{137}{18}\) is about 7.6, so 7 bags fit (126 kilograms) but 8 would be 144 kilograms and push the total over 480.

whyWrong.A: 5 bags is well under the limit and wastes 47 kilograms of the allowance; the question asks for the greatest number that still fits.
whyWrong.B: 6 bags also fits but is not the greatest; 7 bags brings the total to 469 kilograms, still at most 480.
whyWrong.D: 8 bags is 144 kilograms, making the total 487 kilograms, which exceeds the 480-kilogram limit. This is the answer if you round 7.6 up instead of down.

commonMistakes: Rounding the quotient up. For a "greatest number that still fits" question you always round down, whatever the decimal is.
tips: Count only one passenger's mass and you get 8 bags, so check that both passengers are included.

whyCorrect: After s shifts the first rig has drilled 340 + 25s metres and the second has drilled 460 + 15s metres. Setting them equal gives 340 + 25s = 460 + 15s, so 10s = 120 and s = 12 shifts. The question asks for the length drilled, not the number of shifts, so substitute: 340 + 25(12) = 340 + 300 = 640 metres (and 460 + 15(12) = 640 as a check).

whyWrong.A: 300 is the extra distance the first rig drills during those 12 shifts, not its total; the 340 metres already drilled still has to be added.
whyWrong.B: 480 is 40(12), the sum of the two drilling rates times the 12 shifts; the rates are compared, not added, and the head starts still have to be included.
whyWrong.C: 600 is close but corresponds to s = 10.4 for the first rig; check it against the second rig and 460 + 15s = 600 gives s = 9.33, so the two rigs are not at the same point.

commonMistakes: Answering 12, the number of shifts, when the question asks how many metres each rig has drilled.

whyCorrect: The reservoir holds 1,250 + 340h litres after h hours of pumping. Set 1,250 + 340h = 12,450 to get 340h = 11,200, so h is about 32.9 hours of pumping. The pump runs 9 hours a day, so after 3 days it has run 27 hours and after 4 days 36 hours; 32.9 falls inside day 4, so the reservoir first has to be emptied on day 4.

whyWrong.B: 5 comes from forgetting the 1,250 litres already in the reservoir: 12,450 divided by 340 is 36.6 hours, which is 4.07 days and rounds up into day 5.
whyWrong.C: 6 is what you get if the pump is taken to run 6 hours a day rather than 9, since 32.9 divided by 6 is 5.5.
whyWrong.D: 7 uses a 5-hour day, since 32.9 divided by 5 is about 6.6; the question says the pump runs 9 hours each day.

commonMistakes: Reporting 32.9 or 3.66 (the raw hours or days of pumping) instead of the numbered day of the spell.
tips: Count in whole days: 27 hours of pumping by the end of day 3, 36 by the end of day 4.

whyCorrect: Every forging uses the same mass, so find that mass first: 560 - 344 = 216 kilograms went in 12 forgings, which is 216 divided by 12, or 18 kilograms per forging. After 20 forgings the store has used 20(18) = 360 kilograms, leaving 560 - 360 = 200 kilograms.

whyWrong.A: 182 comes from subtracting a further 162 kilograms (9 more forgings' worth) from 344, which counts 21 forgings rather than 20.
whyWrong.C: 216 is the coke used in the first 12 forgings, not what is left after 20.
whyWrong.D: 224 subtracts 8 more forgings from 344 using a rate of 15 kilograms rather than 18, which is what you get from dividing 216 by 14 or similar.

tips: Work out the per-forging rate from the pair of values you are given before extending the model.

whyCorrect: Let g be granite trips and b ballast trips, so g + b = 34 and 8g + 14b = 386. Substituting g = 34 - b gives 8(34 - b) + 14b = 386, that is 272 + 6b = 386, so 6b = 114 and b = 19. Check: 15 granite trips carry 120 tonnes and 19 ballast trips carry 266 tonnes, totalling 386.

whyWrong.A: 13 gives 13(14) + 21(8) = 182 + 168 = 350 tonnes, 36 tonnes short of the total.
whyWrong.B: 15 is the number of granite trips, the other variable; it answers the wrong half of the system.
whyWrong.D: 21 gives 21(14) + 13(8) = 294 + 104 = 398 tonnes, which overshoots 386.

commonMistakes: Solving the system correctly and then reporting g instead of b.

whyCorrect: Expand the product first: \((2w+5)(w-3)=2w^{2}-6w+5w-15=2w^{2}-w-15\) . Now subtract the whole second expression, distributing the minus sign across both of its terms: \(2w^{2}-w-15-w^{2}+4w\) . Combining like terms gives \(w^{2}+3w-15\) .

whyWrong.A: \(w^{2}-5w-15\) comes from subtracting only \(w^{2}\) and then subtracting \(4w\) as well, that is from not flipping the sign of the \(-4w\) term.
whyWrong.B: \(3w^{2}-w-15\) adds the \(w^{2}\) instead of subtracting it, so the expression is treated as a sum rather than a difference.
whyWrong.C: \(w^{2}+3w+15\) has the right variable terms but flips the sign of the constant; \(-15\) is not touched by the subtraction at all.

commonMistakes: Dropping the parentheses around \(w^{2}-4w\) before distributing the minus sign, which leaves \(-4w\) unchanged.

whyCorrect: Set the model equal to the value you want: \(\frac{288}{h+4}=18\) . Multiply both sides by \(h+4\) to clear the fraction, giving \(288=18(h+4)\) , so \(h+4=\frac{288}{18}=16\) and h = 12.

whyWrong.B: 14 comes from dividing 288 by 18 to get 16 and then subtracting 2 instead of the 4 in the denominator.
whyWrong.C: 18 is the moisture percent from the question re-used as the time; substituting it gives \(\frac{288}{22}\) , about 13.1 percent.
whyWrong.D: 20 comes from reading the model as \(\frac{288}{h}+4=18\) , which puts the 4 outside the fraction.

tips: Clear the fraction first; solving \(\frac{a}{x}=b\) by cross-multiplying avoids most of the sign and placement slips here.

whyCorrect: Set \(1{,}600\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{\frac{t}{3}}=100\) and divide both sides by 1,600 to get \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{\frac{t}{3}}=\frac{1}{16}\) . Since \(\frac{1}{16}=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{4}\) , the exponents must match: \(\frac{t}{3}=4\) , so t = 12. In words, the pressure halves every 3 hours and it takes 4 halvings to go from 1,600 to 100.

whyWrong.A: 8 counts the halvings but multiplies by 2 instead of 3, or treats 1,600 as reaching 100 in 3 steps.
whyWrong.C: 16 is 4 halvings times 4 hours, using the wrong time per halving; the exponent \(\frac{t}{3}\) says one halving takes 3 hours.
whyWrong.D: 24 is 8 halvings, which would take the pressure down to \(\frac{1{,}600}{256}=6.25\) pascals, far below 100.

commonMistakes: Setting \(\frac{t}{3}\) equal to 16 rather than recognising \(\frac{1}{16}\) as the fourth power of \(\frac{1}{2}\) .

whyCorrect: Find k from the bell you know: \(500=\frac{k}{1.2^{2}}=\frac{k}{1.44}\) , so k = 720. Then for the 2-metre bell, \(f=\frac{720}{2^{2}}=\frac{720}{4}=180\) hertz.

whyWrong.A: 120 comes from squaring 2 twice or from dividing 720 by 6; check it against \(f=\frac{k}{d^{2}}\) and it needs k = 480.
whyWrong.B: 144 uses \(\frac{720}{5}\) -style arithmetic, or scales 500 by \(\frac{1.44}{5}\) ; it also echoes the 1.44 from the first bell.
whyWrong.D: 300 scales the pitch by the diameters themselves, \(500\times\frac{1.2}{2}\) , treating the relationship as inverse in d rather than in \(d^{2}\) .

tips: With inverse-square variation, doubling the diameter divides the pitch by 4, not by 2.

whyCorrect: Start from \(N=\frac{3A}{2t}\) and multiply both sides by \(2t\) to get \(2tN=3A\) . Now divide both sides by \(2N\) : \(t=\frac{3A}{2N}\) . Notice t was in the denominator, so once it is freed the N it trades places with lands in the denominator instead.

whyWrong.A: \(\frac{2N}{3A}\) is the reciprocal of the answer; it comes from inverting the whole equation but forgetting that only t, not N, is being isolated.
whyWrong.B: \(\frac{3AN}{2}\) multiplies by N instead of dividing, which is what happens if you clear the 2t but then treat N as though it were already on the left.
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{2A}{3N}\) swaps the 2 and the 3, keeping the letters right but inverting the numerical coefficient.

commonMistakes: Trying to move t before clearing the fraction; multiplying both sides by the denominator first makes the rest routine.

whyCorrect: Let w be the width, so the length is 3w + 4 and the area is \(w(3w+4)=644\) . That rearranges to \(3w^{2}+4w-644=0\) , which factors with roots from the quadratic formula: the discriminant is \(16+4(3)(644)=7{,}744=88^{2}\) , so \(w=\frac{-4+88}{6}=14\) . The question asks for the length, so compute 3(14) + 4 = 46 centimetres.

whyWrong.A: 14 is the width, the value of w, not the length the question asks for.
whyWrong.B: 42 is 3 times the width but leaves off the extra 4 centimetres in "4 more than 3 times the width".
whyWrong.D: 52 comes from taking the width as 16, which gives an area of 16(52) = 832 square centimetres, not 644.

commonMistakes: Solving the quadratic and stopping at w; check which dimension the final sentence asks for.
tips: You can also test the choices: 46 times \(\frac{46-4}{3}=14\) gives 644 straight away.

whyCorrect: First convert apples to juice using the given rate: 3,300 kilograms is 300 lots of 11 kilograms, and each lot yields 7 litres, so the crop gives 300(7) = 2,100 litres. Then divide by the cask size: \(\frac{2{,}100}{15}=140\) casks, exactly, so 140 casks are filled completely.

whyWrong.B: 150 divides 3,300 by 22, or applies the cask size to a juice volume of 2,250 litres; it skips the 7-to-11 conversion.
whyWrong.C: 210 is the juice in litres divided by 10, treating the casks as 10-litre casks.
whyWrong.D: 300 is the number of 11-kilogram lots of apples, not the number of casks.

commonMistakes: Dividing the apple mass by the cask size directly, without turning kilograms of apples into litres of juice first.

whyCorrect: Apply the two changes in order to the running total, not to the original figure twice. Falling 25 percent leaves 75 percent: 4,800(0.75) = 3,600 kilograms. Rising 12 percent from there multiplies by 1.12: 3,600(1.12) = 4,032 kilograms.

whyWrong.A: 3,960 raises 3,600 by 10 percent rather than 12 percent.
whyWrong.C: 4,140 is 4,800 times 0.8625, a net multiplier that matches neither order of the two changes; the correct chain 0.75 then 1.12 gives a net 0.84.
whyWrong.D: 4,224 is 4,800(0.88), which applies the 12 percent as a single decrease and loses the 25 percent fall entirely.

commonMistakes: Assuming a 25 percent fall and a 12 percent rise partly cancel; percentages of different bases never simply add.
tips: Chain the multipliers: \(4{,}800\times0.75\times1.12\) .

whyCorrect: "Greatest volume for each hour run" means the largest ratio of litres to hours, so divide each pump's water by its hours rather than comparing the raw totals. Aldergate gives 90,000 divided by 120 = 750 litres per hour, Chalk Down 108,000 divided by 150 = 720, Barrow Fen 148,500 divided by 180 = 825, and Denhill 156,000 divided by 200 = 780. Barrow Fen's 825 litres per hour is the largest.

whyWrong.A: Aldergate raised the least water in total and its rate, 750 litres per hour, is beaten by both Barrow Fen and Denhill.
whyWrong.B: Chalk Down has the lowest rate in the table at 720 litres per hour.
whyWrong.D: Denhill raised the most water overall, 156,000 litres, but it also ran the longest; at 780 litres per hour it is second to Barrow Fen. Picking it means comparing totals instead of rates.

commonMistakes: Reading off the largest number in the water column; the question asks per hour, so the hours column has to be used.

whyCorrect: The phrase "of the casks whose repair called for a new head" fixes the denominator as that column only: 84 + 56 + 60 = 200 casks. Of those, 84 were hogsheads, so the percent is \(\frac{84}{200}=0.42\) , which is 42%.

whyWrong.A: 21% is \(\frac{84}{400}\) , using the grand total of all 400 casks as the denominator instead of the new-head column.
whyWrong.B: 28% is \(\frac{56}{200}\) , the butt share of the new-head column, so it reads the wrong row.
whyWrong.C: 30% is \(\frac{60}{200}\) , the firkin share of the same column.

tips: Underline the phrase that names the group before computing; it tells you the denominator.

whyCorrect: Turn each mean into a total. All 9 bells together weigh 9(284) = 2,556 kilograms, and the 8 bells without the tenor weigh 8(246) = 1,968 kilograms. The tenor is the difference: 2,556 - 1,968 = 588 kilograms.
commonMistakes: Subtracting the means, 284 - 246 = 38, which is only the shift in the average, not the mass of the bell removed.
tips: Whenever a mean changes because an item is added or removed, work with sums: sum = mean times count.

whyCorrect: B and C lie on \(AD\) in order, so the three pieces add to the whole: \(AB+BC+CD=AD\) . That gives 3x + (x + 8) + (2x - 5) = 63, so 6x + 3 = 63, and x = 10. The question asks for \(BC\) , which is x + 8 = 18 metres.

whyWrong.B: 20 is 2x, or the value of \(AB\) minus \(CD\) ; it is not the expression x + 8.
whyWrong.C: 24 is what x + 8 gives if x is taken as 16, which comes from solving 6x + 3 = 63 as 6x = 96.
whyWrong.D: 30 is \(AB=3x\) , the wrong segment.

commonMistakes: Solving for x and reporting it, or reporting the wrong segment; substitute x back into the expression the question names.

whyCorrect: The cable is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose horizontal leg, 14 metres, is adjacent to the 60° angle, so use cosine: \(\cos 60^{\circ}=\frac{14}{L}\) . Since \(\cos 60^{\circ}=\frac{1}{2}\) , L = 28 metres of cable are used. The drum started with 45 metres, so 45 - 28 = 17 metres are left.

whyWrong.A: 11 comes from using \(\tan 60^{\circ}\) to get a length of about 24.2 and subtracting, or from taking the cable as 34 metres.
whyWrong.C: 21 uses \(14\sqrt{3}\approx24.2\) , the height of the nose above the ground, as the cable length rather than the hypotenuse.
whyWrong.D: 31 subtracts the 14-metre ground distance from 45, ignoring the angle entirely.

commonMistakes: Answering 28, the cable length, when the question asks how much is left on the drum.

whyCorrect: Find the volume first: 1.2 times 0.8 times 0.5 = 0.48 cubic metres. Density is given as mass per cubic metre, so multiply: 0.48(2,700) = 1,296 kilograms.
commonMistakes: Adding or averaging the three dimensions instead of multiplying all three, or multiplying only two of them and getting a surface area.

whyCorrect: The barley keeps the same volume, so set the two cylinder volumes equal. In the first silo the volume is \(\pi(2)^{2}(5)=20\pi\) cubic metres. In the second, \(\pi(5)^{2}d=25\pi d\) , so \(25\pi d=20\pi\) and \(d=\frac{20}{25}=0.8\) metre.
commonMistakes: Scaling the depth by the ratio of the radii, \(5\times\frac{2}{5}=2\) , instead of by the ratio of their squares.
tips: \(\pi\) cancels from both sides, so you never need a decimal value for it.

whyCorrect: Each horseshoe costs the same $9, so the number made is the total charge divided by the price of one: 153 divided by 9 = 17. Check it by multiplying back: 9(17) = 153.

whyWrong.B: 18 horseshoes would come to 9(18) = $162, which is $9 more than the farrier was charged.
whyWrong.C: 19 horseshoes would come to 9(19) = $171.
whyWrong.D: 21 horseshoes would come to 9(21) = $189, far above $153.

tips: Multiply your answer by 9 before moving on; a division slip shows up immediately.

whyCorrect: The tin and the copper together make up the bell metal, so 340 + x = 425. Subtract 340 from both sides: x = 425 - 340 = 85 kilograms.

whyWrong.A: 75 added to 340 gives 415 kilograms, 10 short of the stated 425.
whyWrong.C: 95 added to 340 gives 435 kilograms, 10 too much.
whyWrong.D: 105 added to 340 gives 445 kilograms; it comes from subtracting 320 rather than 340.

tips: Add your answer back to 340 and confirm you land on 425 exactly.

whyCorrect: The 15 movements are already done before the w weeks start, so they are a constant, and 4 movements are added in each of those weeks, so they are multiplied by w. That gives 15 + 4w.

whyWrong.A: \(4w-15\) subtracts the finished movements instead of adding them, so it says the total drops below zero in the first weeks.
whyWrong.B: \(15w+4\) swaps the roles: it treats 15 as the weekly rate and 4 as the number already finished.
whyWrong.D: \(19w\) adds 15 and 4 before multiplying, so the 15 already-finished movements get repeated every week.

commonMistakes: Combining the constant and the rate into one number; only the rate is multiplied by w.

whyCorrect: In \(C(m)=38+0.60m\) the number attached to m is the slope, so it tells you how much the charge changes for each extra unit of m. Since m counts minutes and C is in dollars, 0.60 is the extra charge in dollars for each further minute the tug is airborne. The 38 is the part that does not depend on m at all.

whyWrong.A: This describes the constant 38, the flat part of the charge that applies whatever the airborne time.
whyWrong.B: The charge is $38 when m = 0, so this would be 0 minutes, not 0.60.
whyWrong.C: A 38-minute launch costs 38 + 0.60(38) = $60.80, so this misreads 38 as an input rather than as the flat charge.

tips: In \(y=b+mx\) the coefficient of the variable is always a rate: units of y per one unit of x.

whyCorrect: The ladder carries the picker and the bag together, so the load is 78 + a, and "at most 130" means that total can be 130 or less: \(78+a\le 130\) . Subtracting 78 from both sides gives \(a\le 52\) .

whyWrong.A: \(a\ge 52\) reverses the inequality, saying the bag must be at least 52 kilograms, which is the opposite of a safety limit.
whyWrong.B: \(a\le 130\) applies the whole limit to the bag alone and ignores the picker's 78 kilograms.
whyWrong.C: \(a\le 208\) adds 78 to 130 instead of subtracting it, moving the picker's mass to the wrong side.

commonMistakes: Treating "at most" as strictly less than; at most includes the value itself, so the sign is \(\le\) , not <.

whyCorrect: After d days the barrel holds 90 - 7d gallons. Set 90 - 7d = 34, so 7d = 90 - 34 = 56, and d = 8 days.

whyWrong.B: 9 days leaves 90 - 63 = 27 gallons, which is below 34.
whyWrong.C: 12 is roughly 90 divided by 7, the number of days to empty the barrel altogether, not to reach 34 gallons.
whyWrong.D: 14 comes from dividing the 56 gallons drawn off by 4 instead of by the 7 gallons taken each day.

tips: Subtract first to find how much has been drawn off, then divide by the daily amount.

whyCorrect: The cable let out after h hours is 84 + 6h. With h = 5 that is 84 + 6(5) = 84 + 30 = 114 metres.

whyWrong.A: 90 adds 6 only once, as though one hour had passed rather than five.
whyWrong.C: 120 adds 6 six times (84 + 36), counting an extra hour.
whyWrong.D: 126 adds 6 seven times, or comes from multiplying 84 by a rate instead of adding to it.

commonMistakes: Multiplying 84 by 5; the 84 metres are already out and are not repeated each hour.

whyCorrect: Distribute the 3 across both terms inside the parentheses: \(3(2q)=6q\) and \(3(-7)=-21\) . So \(3(2q-7)=6q-21\) .

whyWrong.A: \(6q-7\) multiplies only the first term and leaves the 7 untouched.
whyWrong.B: \(5q-21\) adds 3 and 2 rather than multiplying them.
whyWrong.D: \(2q-21\) multiplies only the constant and leaves the \(2q\) untouched.

commonMistakes: Distributing to just one term inside the parentheses; the factor outside multiplies everything inside.

whyCorrect: \(x^{2}-49\) is a difference of two squares, since \(49=7^{2}\) . A difference of squares always factors as \((x-7)(x+7)\) . Expanding confirms it: the two middle terms \(-7x\) and \(+7x\) cancel, leaving \(x^{2}-49\) .

whyWrong.A: \((x-7)^{2}\) expands to \(x^{2}-14x+49\) , which has an extra \(-14x\) term and the wrong sign on 49.
whyWrong.B: \((x+7)^{2}\) expands to \(x^{2}+14x+49\) , also not a difference of squares.
whyWrong.C: \(x(x-49)\) expands to \(x^{2}-49x\) , which subtracts \(49x\) rather than 49.

tips: Expand any factoring choice you are unsure of; it takes seconds and settles the sign questions.

whyCorrect: Substitute d = 6 and follow the order of operations: square first, then multiply, then add. \(C(6)=5(6)^{2}+40=5(36)+40=180+40=220\) .

whyWrong.A: 100 is \(5(12)+40\) , which uses 2d in place of \(d^{2}\) .
whyWrong.B: 130 is \(5(18)+40\) , which uses 3d in place of \(d^{2}\) .

commonMistakes: Multiplying before squaring, that is computing \((5\times 6)^{2}\) instead of \(5\times 6^{2}\) .

whyCorrect: Set the expression equal to the reading: \(\sqrt{n+7}=5\) . Square both sides to undo the radical: n + 7 = 25. Subtract 7 to get n = 18. Check: \(\sqrt{18+7}=\sqrt{25}=5\) .

whyWrong.B: 25 is \(5^{2}\) , the value of n + 7, reported before the 7 is subtracted.
whyWrong.C: 32 adds 7 to 25 instead of subtracting it, so the 7 is moved the wrong way.
whyWrong.D: 39 comes from squaring and then adding 7 twice over.

tips: Square both sides first; trying to peel off the 7 while it is still under the radical does not work.

whyCorrect: Substitute d = 2 into the model: \(S(2)=81\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{2}=81\times\frac{1}{9}=9\) grams per litre. The base \(\frac{1}{3}\) means the sugar falls to a third of its value each day, so after two days it is a third of a third.

whyWrong.A: 3 is the value after 3 days, one division by 3 too many.
whyWrong.C: 27 is the value after 1 day, so only one third has been taken.
whyWrong.D: 54 subtracts 27 from 81, treating the model as though 27 grams per litre were removed each day instead of the amount being multiplied by \(\frac{1}{3}\) .

commonMistakes: Reading exponential decay as a constant subtraction each day.

whyCorrect: A power of a product raises each factor to that power: \(\left(2x^{3}\right)^{4}=2^{4}\left(x^{3}\right)^{4}\) . Then \(2^{4}=16\) and a power raised to a power multiplies the exponents, so \(\left(x^{3}\right)^{4}=x^{12}\) . The result is \(16x^{12}\) .

whyWrong.A: \(8x^{12}\) uses \(2^{3}\) instead of \(2^{4}\) , applying the wrong exponent to the coefficient.
whyWrong.B: \(2x^{12}\) leaves the coefficient untouched, as though the outer exponent applied only to the variable.
whyWrong.D: \(16x^{7}\) adds the exponents 3 and 4 instead of multiplying them; adding applies when powers are multiplied together, not nested.

tips: Two rules are in play here: distribute the outer exponent over every factor, then multiply nested exponents.

whyCorrect: Cost is the price per kilogram times the number of kilograms: 1.35(40). Since 1.35(4) = 5.40, multiplying by 40 gives $54.

whyWrong.A: $27 is 1.35(20), the cost of half the malt.
whyWrong.B: $29.60 is close to 40 divided by 1.35, which reverses the operation.
whyWrong.C: $48.60 is 1.35(36), so four kilograms are left out.

tips: Multiply by 4 and then shift the decimal one place, rather than multiplying by 40 directly.

whyCorrect: 12 percent means 0.12 of the total, so the number rejected is 0.12(250) = 30 nails. A quick check: 10 percent of 250 is 25 and 1 percent is 2.5, so 12 percent is 25 + 5 = 30.

whyWrong.B: 45 is 18 percent of 250, so the percentage has been read wrong.
whyWrong.C: 88 is the percent of nails kept, not a count of nails at all.
whyWrong.D: 220 is the number of nails kept, that is 250 - 30, rather than the number rejected.

commonMistakes: Answering with the nails that passed; read the last line to see which group is wanted.

whyCorrect: Read the two rows the question names: week 3 shows 52 casks and week 1 shows 38. "How many more" is a subtraction, so 52 - 38 = 14.

whyWrong.A: 7 is the difference between weeks 1 and 2, not weeks 1 and 3.
whyWrong.C: 17 comes from subtracting 35 rather than 38, a borrowing slip in 52 - 38.
whyWrong.D: 21 adds three weekly steps of 7 rather than the two that separate week 1 from week 3.

tips: Point at the two numbers in the table before subtracting; most errors here are row-picking, not arithmetic.

whyCorrect: The question asks only about the winch column, so ignore the aerotow figures entirely. Those values are 14, 11, 23 and 19, and the largest is 23, on Saturday.

whyWrong.A: Thursday had 14 winch launches, the second smallest in that column.
whyWrong.B: Friday had the fewest winch launches, 11; its 16 is the aerotow figure.
whyWrong.D: Sunday has the largest day total (19 + 21 = 40) and the most aerotow launches, but 19 winch launches is fewer than Saturday's 23.

commonMistakes: Comparing row totals when the question names one column.

whyCorrect: The mean is the total divided by how many values there are. Adding: 82 + 95 + 74 + 110 + 88 + 91 = 540. There are 6 anvils, so the mean is 540 divided by 6 = 90 kilograms.
commonMistakes: Dividing by 5 after miscounting the list, or reporting the median (89.5) instead of the mean.
tips: Add the values in pairs that make round numbers (82 + 88, 95 + 74 + 110 + 91) to keep the sum reliable.

whyCorrect: A square corner is a right angle, so the two pieces the scribed line creates must add to 90°. That gives 90 - 34 = 56 degrees.

whyWrong.B: 66 subtracts 34 from 100 rather than from 90.
whyWrong.C: 124 adds 34 to 90 instead of subtracting it.
whyWrong.D: 146 subtracts 34 from 180, treating the corner as a straight angle rather than a right angle.

commonMistakes: Using 180° out of habit; complementary angles sum to 90°, supplementary ones to 180°.

whyCorrect: Lining all six faces means finding the surface area, not the volume. Opposite faces come in matching pairs: 8 by 5 twice, 8 by 3 twice and 5 by 3 twice, so the area is 2(40) + 2(24) + 2(15) = 80 + 48 + 30 = 158 square feet.

whyWrong.A: 120 is the volume, 8(5)(3), in cubic feet; it answers how much the crate holds, not how much felt covers it.
whyWrong.C: 166 is 8 more than the correct total, a slip in adding 40 + 24 + 15 before doubling.
whyWrong.D: 240 doubles the volume, applying the pairing rule to the wrong quantity.

tips: Surface area is always in square units and volume in cubic units; check the units the question asks for.

whyCorrect: An L-shape splits into the two rectangles it is described as. Their areas are 12(5) = 60 and 4(3) = 12 square metres. Since they are joined edge to edge and do not overlap, the total is 60 + 12 = 72 square metres.
commonMistakes: Adding the side lengths and multiplying, for instance (12 + 4)(5 + 3) = 128, which invents floor space the L-shape does not have.

whyCorrect: The side opposite an angle and the hypotenuse are linked by sine: \(\sin 30^{\circ}=\frac{\text{opposite}}{18}\) . Since \(\sin 30^{\circ}=\frac{1}{2}\) , the opposite side is \(\frac{18}{2}=9\) centimetres.
commonMistakes: Using cosine, which gives the other leg, about 15.6 centimetres.
tips: In a 30-60-90 triangle the short leg is always half the hypotenuse, so you can read this one off without a calculator.

whyCorrect: You do not need x and y separately. Subtracting the first equation from the second gives \(3x+y-(x+3y)=23-17\) , that is 2x - 2y = 6, so x - y = 3. Since x is the pale malt and y the crystal malt, the pale malt exceeds the crystal malt by 3 tonnes.

whyWrong.B: 5 matches neither relation the system forces: adding the equations gives x + y = 10 and subtracting them gives x - y = 3.
whyWrong.C: 10 is x + y, the total mass of the blend, not the amount by which one exceeds the other.
whyWrong.D: 13 combines the two results, 10 and 3, instead of choosing the one the question asks for.

tips: When a question asks for a sum or a difference of the variables, try adding or subtracting the equations directly; solving for each variable is often unnecessary.

whyCorrect: Put the given line in slope-intercept form: 2y = -5x + 9, so \(y=-\frac{5}{2}x+\frac{9}{2}\) and the slope is \(-\frac{5}{2}\) . Since f has that same slope and passes through \((-2,13)\) , moving from x = -2 to x = 6 is a run of 8, so the rise is \(-\frac{5}{2}(8)=-20\) . Therefore f(6) = 13 - 20 = -7.

whyWrong.A: -27 uses a slope of -5, reading the coefficient of x in 5x + 2y = 9 as the slope without dividing by 2.
whyWrong.C: 3 uses a run of 4 rather than 8, which happens if you compute 6 - 2 instead of 6 - (-2).
whyWrong.D: 33 uses a slope of \(+\frac{5}{2}\) , dropping the negative sign that comes from moving 5x across the equals sign.

commonMistakes: Reading the slope straight off Ax + By = C; solve for y first, or use \(-\frac{A}{B}\) .

whyCorrect: Work on all three parts at once. Subtracting 4 gives \(-11<-3x\le 9\) . Now divide every part by -3, and because the divisor is negative both inequality signs reverse: \(\frac{11}{3}>x\ge -3\) . Written left to right that is \(-3\le x<\frac{11}{3}\) .

whyWrong.A: \(x<\frac{11}{3}\) keeps only the bound that came from the -7 side and drops the lower bound entirely.
whyWrong.B: \(-3<x\le \frac{11}{3}\) has the right endpoints but the strictness attached to the wrong ends; reversing an inequality carries each sign's strictness with it, so the closed end lands on -3.
whyWrong.D: \(x\ge -3\) keeps only the lower bound and drops the upper one.

commonMistakes: Flipping the signs but forgetting that the endpoint that was included stays included; \(\le\) becomes \(\ge\) , not <.

whyCorrect: The extract itself never changes, only the volume it sits in. There are 0.12(60) = 7.2 units of extract, and after adding x litres of water the total is 60 + x, so \(\frac{7.2}{60+x}=0.09\) . That gives 60 + x = 80, so x = 20.

whyWrong.A: 12 gives a total of 72 litres and a strength of \(\frac{7.2}{72}=10\) percent, still above 9 percent.
whyWrong.B: 15 gives a total of 75 litres and a strength of 9.6 percent.
whyWrong.D: 24 gives a total of 84 litres and a strength of about 8.6 percent, which is weaker than required.

commonMistakes: Multiplying the 9 percent by the original 60 litres; the new concentration applies to the new total volume, not the old one.

whyCorrect: The cost is linear, so find the per-tonne rate from the two given points: \(\frac{3{,}250-1{,}930}{260-140}=\frac{1{,}320}{120}=11\) dollars per tonne. The setup fee is what is left over: 1,930 - 140(11) = 1,930 - 1,540 = $390. Crushing 400 tonnes then costs 390 + 400(11) = 390 + 4,400 = $4,790.
commonMistakes: Scaling 1,930 up by the ratio \(\frac{400}{140}\) , which wrongly assumes the fixed setup fee scales with tonnage too.
tips: Find the rate first, then back out the fixed fee; the fee is the part that stays put.

whyCorrect: Let c be the number of casks, so the number of firkins is 3c. The staves used are cm for the casks and 3cn for the firkins, and together they make T: cm + 3cn = T. Factoring gives \(c(m+3n)=T\) , so \(c=\frac{T}{m+3n}\) .

whyWrong.A: \(\frac{T}{3(m+n)}\) multiplies the cask staves by 3 as well, as though three times as many casks were made too.
whyWrong.B: \(\frac{T}{m+n}\) assumes equal numbers of casks and firkins and ignores the 3 to 1 ratio.
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{3T}{m+3n}\) is the number of firkins, which is three times the number of casks.

tips: Name the smaller quantity as the variable; here casks are the 1 in the 3-to-1 ratio, so calling them c keeps the algebra simple.

whyCorrect: The upper limit comes from the second condition. Dividing \(0.62m\le 3{,}410\) by 0.62 gives \(m\le 5{,}500\) . The first condition, \(m\ge 4{,}000\) , sets a floor and does not affect the greatest value, so the largest mass that satisfies both is 5,500 kilograms.

whyWrong.B: 5,750 fails the second condition: 0.62(5,750) = 3,565, which is more than 3,410.
whyWrong.D: 6,250 gives 0.62(6,250) = 3,875, the furthest above the limit; it comes from dividing 3,410 by about 0.55 rather than 0.62.

tips: When two conditions bound a quantity from opposite sides, the greatest value always comes from the upper bound.

whyCorrect: First find a. From \(2a^{2}-5=45\) you get \(2a^{2}=50\) , so \(a^{2}=25\) and a = 5, taking the positive value as stated. Then \(f(6)=2(6)^{2}-5=72-5=67\) .

whyWrong.A: 45 is f(a) itself, as though adding 1 to the input left the output unchanged.
whyWrong.C: 72 is \(2(6)^{2}\) with the -5 forgotten.
whyWrong.D: 95 doubles 45 and adds 5, applying operations to the output instead of substituting the new input.

commonMistakes: Assuming \(f(a+1)=f(a)+f(1)\) ; that only holds for very special functions, not for a quadratic.

whyCorrect: Factor both parts. The numerator \(x^{2}-x-12\) needs two numbers multiplying to -12 and adding to -1, which are -4 and 3, so it is \((x-4)(x+3)\) . The denominator is a difference of squares, \((x-4)(x+4)\) . Since \(x>4\) the factor \(x-4\) is not zero and cancels, leaving \(\frac{x+3}{x+4}\) .

whyWrong.A: \(\frac{x-3}{x-4}\) factors the numerator as \((x-3)(x+4)\) , which expands to \(x^{2}+x-12\) , the wrong middle sign.
whyWrong.B: \(\frac{x+3}{x-4}\) keeps the numerator's factoring right but cancels the wrong factor of the denominator.
whyWrong.D: \(\frac{x+4}{x+3}\) is the reciprocal of the answer, with numerator and denominator swapped.

tips: Expand your factoring before cancelling; the middle-term sign is where most of these go wrong.

whyCorrect: A quadratic has exactly one real solution when its discriminant is zero. Here a = k, b = -24 and c = 16, so \(b^{2}-4ac=576-64k=0\) . Solving gives 64k = 576 and k = 9. Check: \(9x^{2}-24x+16=(3x-4)^{2}\) , a perfect square.

whyWrong.A: 3 gives a discriminant of 576 - 192 = 384, which is positive, so there would be two solutions.
whyWrong.B: 4 gives 576 - 256 = 320, again positive.
whyWrong.C: 6 gives 576 - 384 = 192, still positive; it comes from dividing 24 by 4 rather than working with \(b^{2}\) .

commonMistakes: Squaring only the 24 and forgetting the 4ac term, or setting the discriminant greater than zero when "exactly one solution" requires it to equal zero.

whyCorrect: Rewrite both sides as powers of 3: \(9^{x+4}=\left(3^{2}\right)^{x+4}=3^{2x+8}\) and \(27^{x}=\left(3^{3}\right)^{x}=3^{3x}\) . With the bases equal the exponents must be equal, so 2x + 8 = 3x and x = 8.

whyWrong.A: 2 comes from multiplying rather than using exponent rules, for instance solving 9(x + 4) = 27x.
whyWrong.B: 4 comes from writing 2(x + 4) = 3x but distributing only to the x, giving 2x + 4 = 3x.
whyWrong.C: 6 does not balance the equation: \(9^{10}=3^{20}\) while \(27^{6}=3^{18}\) .

tips: Whenever both sides are powers of the same small number, rewrite to that common base before comparing exponents.

whyCorrect: Apply the outer exponent to every factor. \(16^{\frac{3}{4}}\) means the fourth root of 16 cubed, that is \(2^{3}=8\) . For the variables, nested exponents multiply: \(x^{8\cdot\frac{3}{4}}=x^{6}\) and \(y^{4\cdot\frac{3}{4}}=y^{3}\) . The result is \(\frac{8x^{6}}{y^{3}}\) .

whyWrong.B: \(\frac{12x^{6}}{y^{3}}\) multiplies 16 by \(\frac{3}{4}\) instead of raising 16 to that power.
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{8x^{11}}{y^{7}}\) adds \(\frac{3}{4}\) -related steps to the exponents rather than multiplying; 8 + 3 = 11 and 4 + 3 = 7 give away the addition.
whyWrong.D: \(\frac{64x^{6}}{y^{3}}\) takes the square root of 16 and cubes it, \(4^{3}=64\) , instead of the fourth root.

commonMistakes: Forgetting that the denominator of a fractional exponent is the root and the numerator is the power.

whyCorrect: The x-intercepts are 8 and 20, so by symmetry the greatest height occurs halfway between them, at x = 14. Substituting gives \(y=a(14-8)(14-20)=a(6)(-6)=-36a\) . Setting that equal to the greatest height, \(-36a=12\) , gives \(a=-\frac{1}{3}\) .

whyWrong.A: \(-\frac{1}{2}\) would come from a product of \(-24\) at the vertex rather than \(-36\) , for instance by using x = 12 instead of the midpoint x = 14.
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{1}{3}\) has the right size but the wrong sign; a positive a opens the parabola upward, which has a lowest point rather than a greatest height.
whyWrong.D: \(-3\) inverts the division, computing \(\frac{-36}{12}\) instead of \(\frac{12}{-36}\) .

tips: For a parabola written in factored form, the vertex sits at the average of the two roots.

whyCorrect: Work with totals rather than means. The original total is 12(18) = 216 millimetres and the new total is 12(18.5) = 222, so the swap added 6 millimetres. The tile that came out was 16, so the tile that went in is 16 + 6 = 22 millimetres.

whyWrong.A: 18.5 is the new mean, not the thickness of any one tile.
whyWrong.B: 20 adds only 4 millimetres to the 16, which is what you get if the 0.5 rise is multiplied by 8 rather than by all 12 tiles.
whyWrong.C: 21 adds 5, using 10 tiles instead of 12.

commonMistakes: Adding the 0.5 change straight onto 16; a 0.5 rise in the mean of 12 values needs 12(0.5) = 6 extra millimetres in the total.

whyCorrect: Percent increase compares the rise to the previous year's figure, so divide each rise by the earlier value. 2019 rose 18 from 120, which is 15 percent; 2020 rose 18 from 138, about 13 percent; 2021 rose 39 from 156, which is 25 percent; 2022 rose 39 from 195, which is 20 percent. The largest is 2021.

whyWrong.A: 2019's 15 percent is smaller than 2021's 25 percent, even though it is the first rise in the table.
whyWrong.B: 2020 has the smallest percent increase of the four, about 13 percent, because the same rise of 18 is measured against a larger base.
whyWrong.D: 2022 has the largest number of bells and the same rise of 39 as 2021, but the base is 195 instead of 156, so the percent increase is only 20 percent.

commonMistakes: Comparing the raw increases; equal increases give smaller percentages as the starting value grows.

whyCorrect: A margin of error attaches to the estimate of the population mean, not to individual values, and it produces a plausible range rather than a certainty. Here that range is 412 minus 9 to 412 plus 9, so 403 to 421 kilograms, and the population is the 1,500 blocks the sample was drawn from.

whyWrong.B: The interval describes where the mean plausibly lies, not where every block lies; individual blocks vary far more widely than the mean does.
whyWrong.C: A sample can never pin the population mean down exactly; that is the entire reason a margin of error is reported.
whyWrong.D: The random selection was made from the 1,500 blocks at this quarry in this month, so nothing can be concluded about blocks at other quarries.

tips: Ask two questions of every margin-of-error choice: does it talk about the mean or about individuals, and does it stay inside the population that was sampled?

whyCorrect: Direct proportion means the rate scales by the ratio of the speeds: at 32 revolutions per minute the pump raises \(3.5\times\frac{32}{20}=5.6\) litres each second. Then convert 15 minutes to 15(60) = 900 seconds and multiply: 5.6(900) = 5,040 litres.

whyWrong.A: 3,150 is 3.5(900), which uses the old rate and ignores the change in wheel speed.
whyWrong.C: 5,600 uses 1,000 seconds rather than the 900 seconds in 15 minutes.
whyWrong.D: 8,064 applies the speed ratio \(\frac{32}{20}\) twice, giving 3.5(2.56)(900).

commonMistakes: Multiplying by 15 instead of 900; the rate is per second while the time is given in minutes.

whyCorrect: The expected fraction that take is \(\frac{7}{12}\) , so multiply that by the number cut: \(\frac{7}{12}\times 456\) . Since 456 divided by 12 is 38, there are 38 groups of 12, and each contributes 7, giving 38(7) = 266 scions.
commonMistakes: Dividing 456 by 7 or multiplying by \(\frac{12}{7}\) , which inverts the ratio and gives a number larger than the scions cut.
tips: Divide by the denominator first when it goes in evenly; 456 divided by 12 keeps the arithmetic in whole numbers.

whyCorrect: Corresponding angles at two parallel lines cut by a transversal are equal, so 3x + 10 = 5x - 30, giving 2x = 40 and x = 20. The angle at the upper beam is therefore 3(20) + 10 = 70 degrees. Its supplement is 180 - 70 = 110 degrees.

whyWrong.A: 70 is the angle at the upper beam itself; the question asks for the angle supplementary to it.
whyWrong.C: 130 comes from solving 2x = 80 rather than 2x = 40, giving x = 40 and 3x + 10 = 130.
whyWrong.D: 150 is the supplement of 30, treating the constant in \(5x-30\) as though it were an angle measure.

commonMistakes: Setting the two expressions supplementary instead of equal; corresponding angles are equal, so the supplement is taken only at the end.

whyCorrect: The volume of a cylinder is \(\pi r^{2}h\) , and here h = 2r, so the volume is \(\pi r^{2}(2r)=2\pi r^{3}\) . Setting \(2\pi r^{3}=128\pi\) gives \(r^{3}=64\) , so r = 4 centimetres.

whyWrong.A: 2 gives a volume of \(2\pi(8)=16\pi\) , far short of \(128\pi\) .
whyWrong.D: 8 is what you get by reading the height as 2 rather than 2r, since \(\pi r^{2}(2)=128\pi\) leads to \(r^{2}=64\) .

commonMistakes: Dividing 128 by 2 and stopping at 64; that is \(r^{3}\) , not r.

whyCorrect: With the right angle at S, \(\sin R=\frac{5}{13}\) means the side opposite R is 5 and the hypotenuse is 13. The Pythagorean triple 5-12-13 gives the side adjacent to R as 12. Since tangent is opposite over adjacent, \(\tan R=\frac{5}{12}\) .

whyWrong.B: \(\frac{12}{13}\) is \(\cos R\) , adjacent over hypotenuse.
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{12}{5}\) inverts the tangent, putting adjacent over opposite; it is \(\tan T\) , the tangent of the other acute angle.
whyWrong.D: \(\frac{13}{5}\) inverts the sine rather than converting it to a tangent.

tips: Sketch the triangle and label all three sides before reading off any ratio; the third side almost always comes from a familiar triple.

whyCorrect: Volume is \(\pi r^{2}h\) , so scaling the radius by 1.5 scales the volume by \(1.5^{2}=2.25\) , and scaling the height by 0.8 scales it by 0.8. Together the second vat holds \(400\times 2.25\times 0.8=720\) litres.
commonMistakes: Scaling the radius by 1.5 rather than by \(1.5^{2}\) , which gives 480 litres, or netting the two percentages to conclude the volume rises by 30 percent.
tips: You never need the actual radius or height; only the scale factors matter.

whyCorrect: Split the day at the point where the rate changes. The first 3 hours produced 3(240) = 720 turves, so the slower spell produced 1,440 - 720 = 720 turves. At 180 an hour that spell lasted 720 divided by 180 = 4 hours. The question asks for the whole day, so the total is 3 + 4 = 7 hours.

whyWrong.A: 4 is only the length of the slower spell; the first 3 hours still have to be added.
whyWrong.B: 6 is 1,440 divided by 240, which applies the fast rate to the entire day.
whyWrong.D: 8 is 1,440 divided by 180, which applies the slow rate to the entire day.

commonMistakes: Averaging the two rates to 210 an hour; the rates apply for different lengths of time, so they cannot simply be averaged.

whyCorrect: The count falls by the same amount each ring, so find that amount from the two rings given: from ring 3 to ring 8 is 5 steps and the count drops 70 - 40 = 30, so each step is 6 billets. Ring 12 is 4 steps above ring 8, so it holds 40 - 4(6) = 40 - 24 = 16 billets.

whyWrong.A: 10 counts 5 steps past ring 8, which lands on ring 13 rather than ring 12.
whyWrong.C: 22 counts only 3 steps past ring 8, landing on ring 11.
whyWrong.D: 28 uses a drop of 3 per ring, which comes from dividing 30 by 10 instead of by the 5 steps between rings 3 and 8.

tips: Count steps between ring numbers, not the ring numbers themselves: rings 3 to 8 are 5 steps apart, not 8.

whyCorrect: Set the two charges equal for s sacks: 65 + 18s = 23s. Subtracting 18s gives 65 = 5s, so s = 13 sacks. The question asks for the amount charged, not the number of sacks, so compute 23(13) = $299 (and 65 + 18(13) = 65 + 234 = $299 as a check).

whyWrong.A: $234 is 18(13), the first merchant's per-sack charge with the $65 delivery fee left out.
whyWrong.B: $260 is 20(13), using a price halfway between $18 and $23 rather than either merchant's actual rate.
whyWrong.C: $286 is 22(13), a slip in the second merchant's price.

commonMistakes: Answering 13, the number of sacks, when the question asks for the amount charged.

whyCorrect: The licence allows 46(2.5) = 115 ewes' worth of stock. The 74 ewes already there use 74 of that, leaving 41 ewes' worth. Each lamb counts as half a ewe, so the marsh takes 41 divided by 0.5 = 82 lambs.

whyWrong.A: 74 lambs count as 37 ewes, giving a total of 111 ewes' worth; that is within the licence but is not the greatest number allowed.
whyWrong.B: 78 lambs count as 39, giving 113 ewes' worth, still short of the 115 permitted.
whyWrong.D: 86 lambs count as 43, giving 117 ewes' worth, which breaks the licence.

commonMistakes: Multiplying the spare capacity by 0.5 instead of dividing by it; because each lamb counts as only half a ewe, the marsh takes twice as many lambs as the spare ewe count.

whyCorrect: Let u be the number of traps in the upper reach. Then the middle reach has 3u and the lower reach has u + 6, and all three add to 56: u + 3u + (u + 6) = 56. That gives 5u + 6 = 56, so 5u = 50 and u = 10. The lower reach therefore has 10 + 6 = 16 traps.
commonMistakes: Reporting u = 10, the upper reach, rather than the lower reach the question names.
tips: Define the variable as the quantity the other two are described in terms of; here everything is stated relative to the upper reach.

whyCorrect: The average cost is the total spent divided by the total sacks. The coarse bark cost 40(12) = $480, and f sacks of fine bark cost 20f, over 40 + f sacks in all, so \(\frac{480+20f}{40+f}=15\) . Multiplying out gives 480 + 20f = 600 + 15f, so 5f = 120 and f = 24.

whyWrong.A: 20 sacks gives a total of $880 over 60 sacks, an average of about $14.67, still below $15.
whyWrong.C: 28 sacks gives $1,040 over 68 sacks, an average of about $15.29.
whyWrong.D: 30 sacks gives $1,080 over 70 sacks, an average of about $15.43.

commonMistakes: Assuming $15 sits halfway between $12 and $20 and so the two quantities are equal; halfway would be $16, and the average being nearer $12 means more coarse sacks than fine.

whyCorrect: Find the rate of change from the two readings: the discharge rises 7.0 - 3.4 = 3.6 while the head rises 2.0 - 0.5 = 1.5, so the slope is 3.6 divided by 1.5 = 2.4 cubic metres per second for each metre of head. To reach 10.6 the discharge must rise 10.6 - 7.0 = 3.6 above the second reading, which takes another 3.6 divided by 2.4 = 1.5 metres of head, giving 2.0 + 1.5 = 3.5 metres.

whyWrong.A: 3.0 divides 7.2 by 2.4 but forgets to add back the 0.5 metres of head at which the first reading was taken.
whyWrong.C: 4.4 divides the discharge 10.6 by the slope 2.4, treating the relationship as directly proportional and ignoring the intercept.
whyWrong.D: 4.8 divides the discharge rise 7.2 by the head difference 1.5, mixing up which quantity the slope divides.

tips: Two points give the slope; then step from one of them rather than starting from zero, because the line does not pass through the origin.

whyCorrect: Complete the square. Factor 2 out of the variable terms: \(2\left(x^{2}-10x\right)+63\) . Half of -10 is -5, and \((x-5)^{2}=x^{2}-10x+25\) , so \(x^{2}-10x=(x-5)^{2}-25\) . Substituting gives \(2(x-5)^{2}-50+63=2(x-5)^{2}+13\) , and since the squared term is never negative the least loss is 13 kilograms.

whyWrong.B: \(2(x-5)^{2}-13\) subtracts the 50 twice, or subtracts it from 63 in the wrong direction; expanding it gives \(2x^{2}-20x+37\) .
whyWrong.C: \(2(x-10)^{2}+13\) uses the full coefficient -10 inside the square rather than half of it; expanding gives \(2x^{2}-40x+213\) .
whyWrong.D: \(2(x-5)^{2}+63\) leaves the 63 untouched, forgetting that completing the square inside the parentheses introduces \(-50\) once the 2 is distributed.

commonMistakes: Forgetting that the 25 added inside the parentheses is multiplied by the 2 outside, so 50 must be taken back out.

whyCorrect: Divide the two given values to get rid of \(N_{0}\) : \(\frac{N(5)}{N(2)}=\frac{1{,}440}{180}=8\) , and that same ratio equals \(b^{3}\) since weeks 2 and 5 are 3 apart. So b = 2, the count doubles each week. Week 4 is one week before week 5, so it is \(\frac{1{,}440}{2}=720\) .

whyWrong.A: 360 is the week-3 value, one doubling too few.
whyWrong.B: 540 uses b = 3, but tripling three times gives a 27-fold rise, not the 8-fold rise the data show.
whyWrong.D: 960 comes from stepping back from 1,440 by a fixed subtraction rather than by dividing by the growth factor.

tips: When two values of an exponential model are given, divide them; the constant \(N_{0}\) cancels and only the base is left.

whyCorrect: Set the two models equal: \(x^{2}-8x+20=5\) , so \(x^{2}-8x+15=0\) , which factors as \((x-3)(x-5)=0\) . The intersections are at x = 3 and x = 5, and both points sit on the line y = 5, so they have the same height and the distance between them is just 5 - 3 = 2.

whyWrong.B: 3 is the x-coordinate of one intersection, not the distance between the two.
whyWrong.C: 4 comes from subtracting 5 from 20 as 16 rather than 15, which gives the perfect square \((x-4)^{2}=0\) and a single point; it is also the axis of symmetry.
whyWrong.D: 5 is the x-coordinate of the other intersection, and it is also the height of the line.

tips: When two points share a y-value, the distance between them is simply the difference of the x-values; no distance formula is needed.

whyCorrect: Use the known reading to find k: \(f(5)=\frac{2(5)+k}{5-3}=\frac{10+k}{2}=7\) , so 10 + k = 14 and k = 4. Then \(f(4)=\frac{2(4)+4}{4-3}=\frac{12}{1}=12\) .

whyWrong.A: 8 is \(\frac{2(4)}{4-3}\) with k left out of the numerator entirely.
whyWrong.B: 10 uses k = 2, which comes from solving 10 + k = 12 rather than 10 + k = 14.
whyWrong.D: 14 keeps the numerator from the x = 5 case, \(2(5)+4\) , while using the new denominator 4 - 3.

commonMistakes: Solving for k and then forgetting to substitute the new x into both the numerator and the denominator.

whyCorrect: Expand the product: \((3x+m)(2x-5)=6x^{2}-15x+2mx-5m=6x^{2}+(2m-15)x-5m\) . For this to match \(6x^{2}-9x-15\) for every x, the constant terms must agree: \(-5m=-15\) , so m = 3. The x terms confirm it, since 2(3) - 15 = -9.

whyWrong.B: 5 is the constant taken from the second factor, \(2x-5\) , not the value of m.
whyWrong.C: 9 is the size of the middle coefficient, not the constant that produces it.
whyWrong.D: 15 comes from reading \(-5m=-15\) as m = 15, dividing on only one side.

tips: Matching the constant terms is usually the fastest route; then use a second pair of coefficients as a check.

whyCorrect: Treat it as a quadratic in \(x^{2}\) . Since \(\left(x^{2}\right)^{2}-13x^{2}+36=0\) factors as \(\left(x^{2}-4\right)\left(x^{2}-9\right)=0\) , you get \(x^{2}=4\) or \(x^{2}=9\) . That gives x = -2, 2, -3 or 3, and the greatest is 3.

whyWrong.A: 2 is a solution but not the greatest one.
whyWrong.B: 2.5 is not a solution at all; it is the average of 2 and 3.
whyWrong.D: 6 is \(\sqrt{36}\) , read off the constant term. Substituting it gives 1,296 - 468 + 36, which is not 0.

commonMistakes: Stopping at \(x^{2}=4\) and \(x^{2}=9\) and reporting 4 or 9; those are values of \(x^{2}\) , not of x.

whyCorrect: Losing 64% of its mass means each turf keeps 100 - 64 = 36% of it, so a dried turf weighs 5(0.36) = 1.8 kilograms. The cart carries 400 dried turves, so the load is 400(1.8) = 720 kilograms.

whyWrong.A: 500 corresponds to dried turves of 1.25 kilograms each, that is keeping only 25% of the original mass.
whyWrong.B: 640 corresponds to 1.6 kilograms each, which is 32% rather than 36%.
whyWrong.C: 700 corresponds to 1.75 kilograms each; the retained fraction is 0.36, not 0.35.

commonMistakes: Multiplying by 0.64, which gives the mass lost rather than the mass kept.

whyCorrect: The roof area is 14(6) = 84 square metres. At 9 bundles for every 2 square metres, that needs \(84\times\frac{9}{2}=378\) bundles. Each load is 120 bundles, and \(\frac{378}{120}=3.15\) , so 3 loads (360 bundles) fall short and the thatcher must order 4.

whyWrong.A: 3 loads give only 360 bundles, 18 short of the 378 needed; the quotient 3.15 has to be rounded up, not down.
whyWrong.C: 5 loads give 600 bundles, a whole load more than necessary, since 4 loads already cover 378.
whyWrong.D: 7 comes from using 9 bundles per square metre instead of per 2 square metres, giving 756 bundles.

commonMistakes: Rounding down when ordering supplies; whenever a part-load is needed, the whole load must be ordered.

whyCorrect: "Per hour" means you have to divide, not compare the raw counts. The rates are 2,760 divided by 6 = 460, 3,150 divided by 7 = 450, 2,000 divided by 5 = 400 and 3,840 divided by 8 = 480. The fastest is the Bank gang at 480 and the slowest is the Hill gang at 400, so the difference is 80 turves per hour.

whyWrong.A: 20 is the gap between 480 and 460, comparing the fastest gang with the second fastest rather than the slowest.
whyWrong.B: 40 is not the gap between any two of the four rates (460, 450, 400 and 480); it usually follows a division slip such as reading 3,840 divided by 8 as 440.
whyWrong.C: 60 is 460 - 400, which treats the Turf gang as the fastest even though the Bank gang's 480 is higher.

commonMistakes: Picking the largest and smallest turf totals; the Bank gang cut the most turves but also worked the longest.

whyCorrect: Convert the mean to a total: 12(25) = 300 kilograms as originally recorded. The one wrong entry was 24 kilograms too low, since 42 - 18 = 24, so the corrected total is 300 + 24 = 324. Dividing by the same 12 hides gives a corrected mean of 27 kilograms.
commonMistakes: Adding 42 to the total and dividing by 13, which counts the corrected hide as an extra hide rather than a replacement.
tips: Only the total changes; the number of values stays at 12, so the mean shifts by \(\frac{24}{12}=2\) .

whyCorrect: The trap is picked from the traps that held eels, so the denominator is that group only: 45 + 75 = 120. Of those, 75 were in the lower reach, so the probability is \(\frac{75}{120}=\frac{5}{8}\) .

whyWrong.A: \(\frac{3}{8}\) is \(\frac{45}{120}\) , the upper reach's share of the traps that held eels, which is the complement of what is asked.
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{5}{12}\) uses a denominator of 180, which is not the size of any group in the table.
whyWrong.D: \(\frac{15}{28}\) is \(\frac{75}{140}\) , which conditions on the lower reach instead: it is the chance a lower-reach trap held eels, not the chance an eel-holding trap was in the lower reach.

commonMistakes: Using all 200 traps as the denominator; the phrase "one of the traps that held eels" restricts the pool before the pick is made.

whyCorrect: The gate post is halfway along, so the distance asked for is half the length of the fence. From (2, -3) to (14, 13) the horizontal change is 12 and the vertical change is 16, so the full length is \(\sqrt{12^{2}+16^{2}}=\sqrt{400}=20\) metres. Half of that is 10 metres.

whyWrong.B: 13 adds the coordinates of the midpoint (8, 5) instead of measuring a distance.
whyWrong.C: 14 averages the two changes, \(\frac{12+16}{2}\) ; distances combine through the Pythagorean theorem, not by averaging.
whyWrong.D: 20 is the whole length of the fence, not the part from (2, -3) to the midpoint.

tips: You can halve the changes first: from (2, -3) the midpoint is 6 across and 8 up, and 6-8-10 is a familiar right triangle.

whyCorrect: Find the whole apron and take the opening out of it. The apron is 18(7) = 126 square metres and the opening is 12(2.5) = 30 square metres, so the paved part is 126 - 30 = 96 square metres.

whyWrong.A: 60 leaves out 66 square metres, more than twice the opening's area.
whyWrong.B: 66 subtracts 60, that is the opening's 30 square metres counted twice.
whyWrong.C: 84 subtracts 42, which is 12 by 3.5 rather than 12 by 2.5.

commonMistakes: Subtracting the opening's dimensions from the apron's before multiplying; area is removed from area, not length from length.

whyCorrect: The angle of 60° is measured between the plank and the vertical face, and the height reached is the leg of the right triangle that lies along that face, so it is adjacent to the 60° angle. That makes it \(12\cos 60^{\circ}=12\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=6\) metres.

whyWrong.B: \(6\sqrt{3}\) is \(12\sin 60^{\circ}\) , which is the distance along the channel floor from the foot of the weir to the bottom of the plank, not the height up the face.
whyWrong.C: 9 matches neither ratio; it is three quarters of the plank's length, which no angle here produces.
whyWrong.D: 12 is the plank's own length, the height it would reach only if it stood flat against the face.

commonMistakes: Assuming the given angle is measured from the ground. Here it is measured from the vertical face, so the roles of sine and cosine are swapped.

whyCorrect: A hemisphere is half a sphere, so its volume is \(\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}=\frac{2}{3}\pi r^{3}\) . With r = 3, \(r^{3}=27\) , so the volume is \(\frac{2}{3}\pi(27)=18\pi\) cubic metres. Since the volume is \(k\pi\) , k = 18.
commonMistakes: Using the full sphere formula and answering 36, or squaring the radius instead of cubing it.
tips: The radius of the circular floor is the radius of the hemisphere, so no extra step is needed to find it.

whyCorrect: The rate is constant, so multiply it by the time: 24(7). Since 24(7) = 168, the engine lifts 168 cubic metres.

whyWrong.A: 144 is 24(6), one minute short.
whyWrong.B: 156 is 24(6.5), which is not a whole number of minutes.
whyWrong.D: 192 is 24(8), one minute too many.

tips: Break the multiplication up if it helps: 24(7) is 20(7) + 4(7) = 140 + 28.

whyCorrect: The charge is 14h, so set 14h = 322 and divide both sides by 14: h = 322 divided by 14 = 23 hurdles. Check: 14(23) = 322.

whyWrong.A: 21 hurdles would come to 14(21) = $294.
whyWrong.C: 26 hurdles would come to 14(26) = $364.
whyWrong.D: 28 hurdles would come to 14(28) = $392.

tips: Multiply your answer back by 14; every wrong choice here fails that check immediately.

whyCorrect: The growth is the same each year, so it is the total rise divided by the number of years between the two counts. The stock rose 3,000 - 1,400 = 1,600 rods over 6 - 2 = 4 years, so it grew 1,600 divided by 4 = 400 rods a year.

whyWrong.A: 250 a year would leave 1,400 + 4(250) = 2,400 rods after 6 years, not 3,000.
whyWrong.B: 320 divides 1,600 by 5 rather than by the 4-year gap; it gives 2,680 rods after 6 years.
whyWrong.C: 350 gives 1,400 + 4(350) = 2,800 rods after 6 years.

commonMistakes: Dividing by 6 instead of by 4; the years that matter are the ones between the two readings, not the year number itself.

whyCorrect: The 130 bundles are already cut, so they are a constant that does not repeat. The 24 bundles are cut on each of the d days, so they are multiplied by d. The total is \(24d+130\) .

whyWrong.B: \(130d+24\) reverses the roles, treating 130 as the daily rate and 24 as the amount already cut.
whyWrong.C: \(154d\) adds the constant to the rate before multiplying, which counts the 130 already-cut bundles again every day.
whyWrong.D: \(130-24d\) subtracts, which would describe a stock being used up rather than a tally growing.

tips: Test the expression at d = 0: it should give 130, the amount already cut.

whyCorrect: "Never more than 2,400" sets an upper limit and allows the value 2,400 itself, since a charge of exactly 2,400 kilograms is not more than 2,400. That is \(m\le 2{,}400\) .

whyWrong.A: \(m<2{,}400\) excludes a charge of exactly 2,400 kilograms, which the rule permits.
whyWrong.C: \(m\ge 2{,}400\) reverses the limit, requiring at least that much.
whyWrong.D: \(m>2{,}400\) describes exactly the charges the rule forbids.

commonMistakes: Reading "more than" as the boundary itself; the forbidden values start above 2,400, so 2,400 is allowed.

whyCorrect: Add the two equations so that b cancels: (a + b) + (a - b) = 40 + 6 gives 2a = 46, so a = 23. Substituting back gives b = 17, and both original equations check out.
commonMistakes: Subtracting the equations instead, which eliminates a and gives b = 17 — the other variable.
tips: When one equation has +b and the other -b, adding them is the fastest way through.

whyCorrect: In C = 9n + 24 the term 24 has no n attached to it, so it does not change with the size of the order. It is added once no matter how many baskets there are, which makes it a fixed charge on every order. The 9 is what changes with n.

whyWrong.A: The per-basket charge is 9, the number multiplied by n.
whyWrong.C: Nothing in the model prices baskets at $9 for a group; 9 is the cost of one basket, so $9 buys one.
whyWrong.D: The model has no maximum: as n grows, C grows without limit.

tips: In C = mn + b, the term without the variable is the fixed part and the coefficient of the variable is the per-unit rate.

whyCorrect: The total is the sum of the two expressions, so add like terms separately: \(4x+6x=10x\) and 15 + (-7) = 8. The total is \(10x+8\) .

whyWrong.B: \(10x+22\) adds 15 and 7 as though both were positive; the sides use \(6x-7\) , so the constant being added is -7.
whyWrong.C: \(10x-8\) subtracts the two expressions instead of adding them.
whyWrong.D: \(24x-105\) multiplies the terms rather than adding them; a total is a sum.

commonMistakes: Combining an x term with a constant. Only \(4x\) and \(6x\) can be added together, and only 15 and -7.

whyCorrect: Substitute n = 6 into both terms: \(6^{2}=36\) and 4(6) = 24. Adding gives \(P(6)=36+24=60\) .

whyWrong.A: 40 is 36 + 4, which adds 4 rather than 4n.
whyWrong.B: 52 is \(6^{2}+4^{2}\) , squaring the 4 instead of multiplying it by n.
whyWrong.D: 72 doubles \(6^{2}\) , treating the second term as another \(n^{2}\) .

tips: Substitute the value everywhere n appears, then follow the order of operations: powers first, then products, then the sum.

whyCorrect: Factor: you need two numbers multiplying to -24 and adding to 5, which are 8 and -3, so \(x^{2}+5x-24=(x+8)(x-3)\) . Setting each factor to zero gives x = -8 and x = 3, and the greater of the two is 3.

whyWrong.A: -24 is the constant term of the equation, not a solution; substituting it gives a very large positive value.
whyWrong.B: -8 is the other solution, the lesser of the two.
whyWrong.C: -3 comes from factoring as \((x+3)(x-8)\) , which expands to \(x^{2}-5x-24\) with the wrong middle sign.

commonMistakes: Taking the signs of the factors from the constant alone; the middle coefficient decides which of the pair is negative.

whyCorrect: Substitute t = 6: \(R(6)=\frac{48}{6}+5\) . Since 48 divided by 6 is 8, the rating is 8 + 5 = 13.

whyWrong.A: 11 divides 48 by 8 rather than by the 6 hours given.
whyWrong.C: 15 would require \(\frac{48}{t}\) to be 10, that is dividing 48 by 4.8.
whyWrong.D: 53 adds 48 and 5 without dividing at all.

commonMistakes: Adding the 5 into the numerator; the 5 sits outside the fraction, so it is added only after the division.

whyCorrect: Multiply the coefficients and add the exponents, because the same base is being multiplied: 3(5) = 15 and \(x^{4}\cdot x^{3}=x^{4+3}=x^{7}\) . The product is \(15x^{7}\) .

whyWrong.B: \(15x^{12}\) multiplies the exponents; that rule applies to a power raised to a power, not to a product.
whyWrong.C: \(8x^{7}\) adds the coefficients 3 and 5 rather than multiplying them.
whyWrong.D: \(8x^{12}\) makes both errors at once, adding the coefficients and multiplying the exponents.

tips: Coefficients multiply, exponents add — the two operations are swapped from what most people expect.

whyCorrect: The base \(\frac{1}{2}\) means the mass halves each day, so after 3 days it has halved three times: 640, then 320, then 160, then 80. Algebraically, \(M(3)=640\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{3}=\frac{640}{8}=80\) kilograms.

whyWrong.A: 20 halves five times, \(\frac{640}{32}\) .
whyWrong.B: 40 halves four times, \(\frac{640}{16}\) .
whyWrong.C: 64 divides 640 by 10, which is not what the model says happens each day.

commonMistakes: Multiplying the exponent by the base, that is dividing 640 by 6 instead of by \(2^{3}\) .

whyWrong.D: 90 is 20% of 450, which is 18% rounded to a friendlier figure.

tips: Build the percentage from 10% and 1%; it is faster than long multiplication and easier to check.

whyCorrect: 96 bushels is 96 divided by 8 = 12 lots of 8 bushels. Each lot gives 3 sacks, so the mill grinds 12(3) = 36 sacks.
commonMistakes: Inverting the ratio and computing \(96\times\frac{8}{3}\) , which gives 256 — more sacks than bushels, which cannot be right here.
tips: Check the direction of a rate by asking whether the answer should be bigger or smaller than the number you started with.

whyCorrect: Add all four grades: 46 + 58 = 104, then 104 + 39 = 143, then 143 + 67 = 210 hurdles.

whyWrong.A: 190 is 20 short, the result of reading 58 as 38.
whyWrong.B: 200 is 10 short, the result of reading 39 as 29.
whyWrong.D: 220 is 10 over, the result of reading 67 as 77.

tips: Add in pairs and keep a running total written down; misreading one row is the usual cause of an error here.

whyCorrect: The median needs the values in order first: 9, 9, 11, 12, 14, 17, 20. With seven values the median is the fourth one, and that is 12.

whyWrong.A: 9 is the smallest value and also the most common one, the mode, not the middle one.
whyWrong.C: 13 is roughly the mean, since the seven values total 92 and 92 divided by 7 is about 13.1.
whyWrong.D: 14 is the fifth value in the ordered list and the first in the list as recorded; with seven values the middle position is the fourth.

commonMistakes: Taking the middle of the list as written; a median is only defined after sorting.

whyCorrect: If 24 of the 40 passed, then 40 - 24 = 16 failed. The fraction that failed is \(\frac{16}{40}\) , and dividing both parts by 8 gives \(\frac{2}{5}\) .

whyWrong.B: \(\frac{3}{5}\) is \(\frac{24}{40}\) , the fraction that passed.
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{2}{3}\) is \(\frac{16}{24}\) , comparing the failures with the passes rather than with all 40 hurdles.
whyWrong.D: \(\frac{1}{4}\) is \(\frac{10}{40}\) and matches no count in the question.

commonMistakes: Answering with the group that is named in the question rather than the one it asks about; 24 is the passes, and the question asks about failures.

whyCorrect: Angles that meet around a single point add to 360°. So 145 + 132 + x = 360, giving x = 360 - 277 = 83.

whyWrong.A: 53 comes from using 330° as the total around the point.
whyWrong.B: 63 comes from using 340°.
whyWrong.C: 73 comes from using 350°.

commonMistakes: Using 180°, which is the total for angles on a straight line; a full turn around a point is 360°.

whyCorrect: For a rectangle, area = length times width, so width = area divided by length. That is 84 divided by 12 = 7 metres.

whyWrong.A: 6 metres would give an area of 12(6) = 72 square metres.
whyWrong.B: 6.5 metres would give 78 square metres.
whyWrong.D: 8 metres would give 96 square metres.

tips: Multiply your width back by 12 and confirm you get 84.

whyCorrect: The straight edge of a semicircle is its diameter, so the radius is 8 divided by 2 = 4 metres. A semicircle is half a circle, so its area is \(\frac{1}{2}\pi r^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\pi(16)=8\pi\) square metres. Since the area is \(k\pi\) , k = 8.
commonMistakes: Using 8 as the radius, which gives \(32\pi\) , or forgetting to halve the circle's area.

whyCorrect: Sine is the side opposite the angle divided by the hypotenuse. The side opposite A is 7 and the hypotenuse is 25, so \(\sin A=\frac{7}{25}\) . No other side is needed.

whyWrong.B: \(\frac{24}{25}\) is \(\cos A\) , using the adjacent side of 24 that the Pythagorean theorem supplies.
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{7}{24}\) is \(\tan A\) , opposite over adjacent.
whyWrong.D: \(\frac{25}{7}\) inverts the sine ratio, putting the hypotenuse on top.

tips: Sine and cosine always have the hypotenuse in the denominator, so a ratio greater than 1 is never one of them.

whyCorrect: A solution has to satisfy both equations, so substitute x = 2 and y = 5 into each. The first gives 2p + 4(5) = 26, so 2p = 6 and p = 3. The second gives 3(2) - q(5) = 1, so 6 - 5q = 1, giving 5q = 5 and q = 1. Therefore p + q = 4.

whyWrong.A: 3 is p on its own; the question asks for the sum.
whyWrong.C: 5 would need q = 2, but then 3(2) - 2(5) = -4, not 1.
whyWrong.D: 7 would need q = 4, giving 6 - 20 = -14 in the second equation.

tips: When a solution is handed to you, substitute rather than solve; the unknown constants drop out one equation at a time.

whyCorrect: Two points give the slope: \(\frac{31-7}{10-2}=\frac{24}{8}=3\) . Using the point (2, 7), g(x) = 7 + 3(x - 2) = 3x + 1. Setting 3x + 1 = 100 gives 3x = 99 and x = 33.

whyWrong.A: 25 comes from dividing 100 by 4, using a slope of 4 rather than 3.
whyWrong.C: 31 is \(\frac{100-7}{3}\) , which uses the rise from g(2) but forgets to add back the 2; it is also the value g(10) copied from the stem.

commonMistakes: Dividing the target output by the slope without accounting for the intercept.

whyCorrect: Clear the fraction across the whole chain by multiplying every part by 4: \(12\le 2x-5\le 28\) . Add 5 to every part: \(17\le 2x\le 33\) . Divide by 2: \(8.5\le x\le 16.5\) , so the greatest value is 16.5.

whyWrong.A: 8.5 is the least possible value, the other end of the range.
whyWrong.B: 12.5 is the midpoint of the range, not either endpoint.
whyWrong.C: 14.5 would need \(\frac{2x-5}{4}\) to equal 6 rather than the stated upper limit of 7.

commonMistakes: Working on only one of the two inequalities; every operation has to be applied to all three parts.

whyCorrect: Notice that 5 sacks of wheat and 4 of barley is exactly half of (4w + 3b) + (6w + 5b) = 10w + 8b. So the answer is half the sum of the two given times: \(\frac{62+98}{2}=80\) minutes. Solving the system confirms it: b = 10 and w = 8, so 5(8) + 4(10) = 80.

whyWrong.B: 84 does not fit the rates: with w = 8 and b = 10, 5 sacks of wheat and 4 of barley take exactly 80 minutes.
whyWrong.C: 90 is roughly the average of 80 and 98 and does not follow from the two grinding rates.
whyWrong.D: 98 is the second grinding time copied from the stem, which is for 6 sacks of wheat and 5 of barley.

tips: Before solving a system, check whether the requested combination is a simple sum, difference or average of the ones you are given.

whyCorrect: At planting, t = 0, so the bed starts with S(0) = p rods. Half of that is \(\frac{p}{2}\) , so set \(p-qt=\frac{p}{2}\) . That gives \(qt=\frac{p}{2}\) , so \(t=\frac{p}{2q}\) .

whyWrong.A: \(\frac{2p}{q}\) solves qt = 2p, doubling the starting stock rather than halving it.
whyWrong.B: \(\frac{p}{q}\) is the time until the model reaches zero rods, which is twice as long as the time to reach half.
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{q}{2p}\) inverts the fraction; check the units — dividing rods by rods per year has to leave years, so p must be on top.

tips: Substitute t = 0 first to identify the starting value; everything else is measured against it.

whyCorrect: Work in minutes: 26 hours is 1,560 minutes. If s baskets are square then 40 - s are round, and the time is 45s + 20(40 - s) = 800 + 25s, which must be at most 1,560. So \(25s\le 760\) , giving \(s\le 30.4\) , and since s is a whole number the greatest is 30.

whyWrong.B: 32 square baskets and 8 round take 32(45) + 8(20) = 1,600 minutes, 40 minutes over the time available.
whyWrong.C: 34 square and 6 round take 1,530 + 120 = 1,650 minutes.
whyWrong.D: 39 square and 1 round take 1,755 + 20 = 1,775 minutes, far beyond 1,560.

commonMistakes: Dividing 1,560 by 45 and answering 34; that ignores the requirement that exactly 40 baskets be finished, so the round baskets take time too.

whyCorrect: Clear both fractions at once by multiplying every term by 6, the least common denominator: \(2(2x+7)-3(x-4)=30\) . Expanding gives 4x + 14 - 3x + 12 = 30, so x + 26 = 30 and x = 4.
commonMistakes: Distributing the minus sign to only the first term of \(x-4\) ; the whole second fraction is subtracted, so \(-3(x-4)\) becomes \(-3x+12\) .
tips: Multiply through by the least common denominator before expanding; it removes both fractions in one step.

whyCorrect: Build each composition separately. \(g(f(x))=(4x+1)^{2}-3(4x+1)=16x^{2}+8x+1-12x-3=16x^{2}-4x-2\) . And \(f(g(x))=4\left(x^{2}-3x\right)+1=4x^{2}-12x+1\) . Subtracting the second from the first, and distributing the minus across all three of its terms, gives \(12x^{2}+8x-3\) .

whyWrong.A: \(12x^{2}+8x-1\) adds the constant of \(f(g(x))\) instead of subtracting it: \(-2-1=-3\) , not \(-2+1\) .
whyWrong.C: \(12x^{2}-8x-3\) subtracts the x terms in the wrong order; \(-4x-(-12x)\) is \(+8x\) .
whyWrong.D: \(20x^{2}-4x-1\) adds the two compositions rather than subtracting one from the other.

commonMistakes: Assuming \(g(f(x))\) and \(f(g(x))\) are the same; the order of composition matters, which is exactly what this difference measures.

whyCorrect: Split the numerator so that part of it matches the denominator: \(6x+19=6(x+3)+1\) , since 6(x + 3) = 6x + 18. Dividing through by x + 3 gives \(6+\frac{1}{x+3}\) , so k = 1.

whyWrong.A: -1 comes from writing 6x + 19 as 6(x + 3) - 1, which would need the numerator to be 6x + 17.
whyWrong.B: 0 treats 19 as 18, which would make the expression exactly 6 with no remainder.
whyWrong.D: 3 is the constant from the denominator, not the remainder left over in the numerator.

tips: Multiply the whole number part by the denominator and see what is left; here 6(x + 3) leaves 1.

whyCorrect: Write both sides as powers of 3: \(9^{x+1}=3^{2(x+1)}=3^{2x+2}\) and \(27^{x-1}=3^{3(x-1)}=3^{3x-3}\) . Equal bases mean equal exponents, so 2x + 2 = 3x - 3, giving x = 5.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to distribute the 2 and the 3 across the whole exponent; both x + 1 and x - 1 are multiplied in full.

whyCorrect: A quadratic with a positive leading coefficient takes its least value at its vertex, and for \(x^{2}+px+q\) that is at \(x=-\frac{p}{2}\) . Setting \(-\frac{p}{2}=5\) gives p = -10. Then f(1) = 1 + p + q = 1 - 10 + q = 9, so q = 18.

whyWrong.A: 9 is f(1) copied as though it were the constant term; the constant term is f(0), not f(1).
whyWrong.B: 14 adds the vertex position 5 to f(1) = 9, which mixes an input with an output.
whyWrong.D: 25 is \(5^{2}\) , the square of the vertex position, which plays no part in finding q.

tips: The vertex formula \(x=-\frac{p}{2}\) pins down p first; only then does the given point pin down q.

whyCorrect: Group the four terms in pairs: \(2x^{3}+3x^{2}\) gives \(x^{2}(2x+3)\) , and \(-8x-12\) gives \(-4(2x+3)\) . The shared factor 2x + 3 comes out, leaving \(\left(2x+3\right)\left(x^{2}-4\right)\) , and \(x^{2}-4\) is a difference of squares, so the full factoring is \((x-2)(x+2)(2x+3)\) .

whyWrong.A: \((x-2)^{2}(2x+3)\) repeats the factor x - 2 instead of pairing it with x + 2; expanding gives \(2x^{3}-5x^{2}-4x+12\) .
whyWrong.B: \((x-3)(x+2)(2x+2)\) expands to \(2x^{3}-14x-12\) , which has no \(x^{2}\) term at all.
whyWrong.C: \(\left(x^{2}+4\right)(2x-3)\) expands to \(2x^{3}-3x^{2}+8x-12\) , with the wrong signs on the middle two terms; \(x^{2}+4\) also does not factor further over the real numbers.

tips: Factoring by grouping works when the two pairs leave the same bracket; if they do not, try a different pairing before giving up.

whyCorrect: An absolute value equation splits into two cases. If 2x - 7 is positive, 2x - 7 = x + 1 gives x = 8. If it is negative, 7 - 2x = x + 1 gives 3x = 6 and x = 2. Both check out in the original equation: at x = 8, \(|2(8)-7|=9\) and x + 1 = 9; at x = 2, \(|2(2)-7|=3\) and x + 1 = 3. The sum is 8 + 2 = 10.

whyWrong.A: 6 is 8 - 2, the difference of the two solutions rather than their sum.
whyWrong.B: 8 is the larger solution alone; the negative case gives a second valid solution.
whyWrong.D: 16 doubles the solution x = 8, as though the equation had that root twice.

commonMistakes: Solving only the positive case. Always set up both, then check each candidate in the original equation.

whyCorrect: Work in cutter-days. The bed takes 6(15) = 90 cutter-days of work, and that total does not change. To finish in 9 days you need 90 divided by 9 = 10 cutters. The gang already has 6, so 4 must be added.

whyWrong.B: 5 added would make 11 cutters, which would finish the bed in about 8.2 days, sooner than the 9 required.
whyWrong.C: 6 added would make 12 cutters and finish in 7.5 days; 6 is also just the original gang size repeated.
whyWrong.D: 10 is the total number of cutters needed, not the number that has to be added to the 6 already there.

commonMistakes: Scaling the number of cutters in the same direction as the days; fewer days needs more cutters, so the relationship is inverse.

whyCorrect: First find which workshop has the greater proportion of failures, which means comparing failures to that workshop's own total. Osier Green failed 32 out of 200, or 16%, while Sedge Fen failed 42 out of 150, or 28%. Sedge Fen has the greater proportion, and it had 42 failures against Osier Green's 32, so the difference is 10.

whyWrong.A: 8 matches no pair of figures in the table; the two failure counts are 32 and 42.
whyWrong.C: 12 is the difference between the two failure percentages, 28% and 16%, not between the numbers of failed hurdles.
whyWrong.D: 14 comes from mixing the two kinds of figure, for instance subtracting the 28% from the count of 42.

commonMistakes: Picking the workshop with more failures outright; Sedge Fen also made fewer hurdles, which is why the proportion has to be computed.

whyCorrect: Usable rods are the rods cut times the percentage not rejected, so compute each one. Willow Ham gives 4,200(0.85) = 3,570; Long Drove gives 3,800(0.94) = 3,572; North Rhyne gives 4,500(0.79) = 3,555; Sedge Bank gives 4,000(0.89) = 3,560. Long Drove is highest, by a narrow margin.

whyWrong.A: Willow Ham yields 3,570, two rods short of Long Drove despite cutting 400 more.
whyWrong.C: North Rhyne cut the most rods, 4,500, but its 21% rejection rate leaves the smallest yield, 3,555.
whyWrong.D: Sedge Bank yields 3,560, third of the four.

commonMistakes: Choosing the bed with the most rods cut or the lowest rejection rate on its own; the yield depends on both, so all four have to be worked out.

whyCorrect: There are 15 rods in all, 6 of them brown, so the first rod is brown with probability \(\frac{6}{15}\) . Because that rod is not put back, only 14 rods remain and 5 of them are brown, so the second is brown with probability \(\frac{5}{14}\) . Multiply: \(\frac{6}{15}\times\frac{5}{14}=\frac{30}{210}=\frac{1}{7}\) .
commonMistakes: Using \(\frac{6}{15}\) twice, which would be right only if the first rod were put back; without replacement both the numerator and the denominator drop by 1.

whyCorrect: The mill keeps 1 sack in every 16, so 27 sacks of toll means 27 lots of 16, that is 27(16) = 432 sacks ground in all. The customers get everything except the toll, so they receive 432 - 27 = 405 sacks.

whyWrong.B: 416 is 26(16), one lot short of the 27 lots the toll represents.
whyWrong.C: 432 is the total ground that week, before the toll is taken out.
whyWrong.D: 459 adds the toll to the total instead of subtracting it.

commonMistakes: Reading "1 in every 16" as 1 kept for every 16 returned; it means 1 kept out of every 16 ground, so 15 of every 16 go back.

whyCorrect: The shaft is a cylinder, so the volume is proportional to the depth. A depth of 4 metres holds \(36\pi\) cubic metres, so each metre of depth holds \(\frac{36\pi}{4}=9\pi\) cubic metres. Raising the level 1.5 metres therefore takes \(1.5\times 9\pi=13.5\pi\) cubic metres.

whyWrong.A: \(9\pi\) is the volume of just one metre of depth, so it leaves out the extra half metre.
whyWrong.B: \(12\pi\) divides \(36\pi\) by 3, which would be the volume of a rise of about 1.33 metres.
whyWrong.D: \(18\pi\) is the volume of a 2-metre rise.

tips: You never need the radius here; the ratio of volumes equals the ratio of depths for a cylinder of constant width.

whyCorrect: Sides in the ratio 3 to 4 with a right angle make a 3-4-5 triangle, and the longest side is the hypotenuse, so 5k = 45 and k = 9. The legs are 3(9) = 27 and 4(9) = 36. Area is half the product of the legs: \(\frac{1}{2}(27)(36)=486\) square centimetres.

whyWrong.A: 405 is \(\frac{1}{2}(45)(18)\) , which uses the hypotenuse as one of the sides forming the right angle.
whyWrong.C: 540 is \(\frac{1}{2}(45)(24)\) , again treating the 45-centimetre side as a leg.
whyWrong.D: 648 is \(\frac{1}{2}(36)(36)\) , using the longer leg twice.

commonMistakes: Applying the ratio 3 to 4 to a leg and the hypotenuse; the ratio is given for the two shorter sides, which makes the third side the 5 in the triple.

whyCorrect: \(\sin A=\frac{5}{13}\) with a hypotenuse of 26 means the side opposite A is \(26\times\frac{5}{13}=10\) . The 5-12-13 triple scaled by 2 gives the other leg as 24. The two legs meet at the right angle, so the area is \(\frac{1}{2}(10)(24)=120\) square centimetres.

whyWrong.A: 60 is \(\frac{1}{2}(10)(12)\) , pairing the scaled leg 10 with the unscaled 12 instead of 24.
whyWrong.B: 96 would need legs multiplying to 192; the legs here are 10 and 24.
whyWrong.D: 156 is \(\frac{1}{2}(26)(12)\) , using the hypotenuse as one of the legs.

tips: Scale the whole triple at once: hypotenuse 26 is 2 times 13, so every side doubles.

whyCorrect: The legs are in the ratio 3 to 4 and the shorter is 1.5 metres, so the longer is \(1.5\times\frac{4}{3}=2\) metres. The triangular cross-section has area \(\frac{1}{2}(1.5)(2)=1.5\) square metres. Since the cross-section is the same all along, multiply by the length: 1.5(20) = 30 cubic metres.

tips: For any prism, volume is the area of the cross-section times the length.
